newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU Commission tightens rubbish dump rules.
newsitem.headline: EU Commission tightens rubbish dump rules.

text.p: The European Commission agreed tighter rules for EU rubbish dumps on Wednesday, including targets for cutting the amount of household waste sent to tips and a ban on the mixed dumping of hazardous and non-toxic trash.

"The proposal for a directive on landfill waste has been adopted," Commission official Christine Dalby told a news conference, adding that the plan was a major improvement on one thrown out by the European Parliament last year.

She said the new rules would limit the allowed share of biodegradable municipal waste sent to dumps to three quarters of generated waste in 2002, one half in 2005 and one quarter by the year 2010, though the earliest figure would not be compulsory.

The proposal, which must pass European Parliament and national government scrutiny before adoption, would also require pre-treatment of waste intended for landfill, a ban on dumping tyres and a hike in dumping prices to include pollution effects, dump closure and aftercare costs.

"This provision aims at restoring the balance between the costs of landfilling of waste, which at present tend to be too low, and the costs of other treatment methods, such as environmentally sound recovery operations, for which the costs are relatively high," the draft text said.
Dalby said the countries likely to be most affected by the proposal would be Britain, Ireland, Greece, Portugal and Spain -- those currently most dependent on landfill dumps.

The problem of poor dump regulatian was clearly illustrated last September in Spain, when a bulging waste tip near La Coruna burst its banks killing one person and posing serious health risks to local inhabitants.

Less spectacularly, landfills can also cause severe soil and water pollution while the rotting of their organic content creates methane, an explosive gas which is also a powerful contributor to the atmospheric greenhouse effect.

The European Parliament received 38 complaints about EU landfills in 1995 and 1996, mainly in Ireland, Italy, Spain and Portugal. The Commission has had another 60 complaints since 1989, these ones concerning dumps in the same countries along with ones in Belgium, Britain, France, Germany and Greece.

Euro-MP David Bowe, whose critical report on the proposal led to its rejection by the assembly, told Reuters on Wednesday he would be looking for tighter definitions on derogations for small islands and sparsely populated regions in the new text.
Dalby said proposed exceptions would cover no more than one percent of the EU's total waste mountain.
Bowe was also concerned that the definition of pre-treatment be sufficiently broad to encourage processes other than burning.

"Crucial will be if they have set a limit for the percentage of carbon in waste that can be landfilled. If it's below a certain level it will virtually mandate that you have to burn waste before it goes into landfill," he said.
"We are not keen on the idea of incineration, we would prefer recycling, recovery or composting," he said.
